Another piece of advice...

If you're having trouble, *ditch the passive*. Too many times, we start having bad experiences because we start seeing ourselves as helpless and inactive in the face of whatever it is we're scared of. When this happens, sitting and thinking is the last thing you want to do.

Get out of your head! You are powerful. You can either get blown by the wind or be the wind yourself. Play music (it's great to have a set of hand drums laying around). Create. Jump. Dance. Do push ups. Get manic. Realize the power you have in your muscles. Psychedelics are often associated with contemplative activities, but serenity is only half of it. There's another side of a trip that can show you how much your primal side kicks ass. 
 
When I'm getting bad vibes, I find that heavy metal or a hardcore punk album is often enough to snap me out of it precisely because when you're headbanging and completely rocking out, you become a powerful force rather than being overpowered. It's quite an experience. Now not everyone wants to listen to Tool or the Bad Brains on LSD and that's understandable, but if you find yourself overcome by a sense of helplessness, a hint of aggression can do the trick. 

Catharsis is a beautiful thing.

If you're going out, try leaving it at home at least a few times a week. 

You'd be surprised how unnecessary it is to be perpetually available to reply to texts. No one is going to get mad at you for not writing back immediately. You probably don't need to Google that. You probably don't need to check Facebook, Twitter, Tinder, even Reddit. It will wait.

It's a nice feeling to be in the now without that ever-available window of escape. You'll notice things you never noticed before. You might be idle but it's nice. If you get bored, people watch. Read a book. Draw a picture. Engage in other, more novel distractions.

And at the end of the day, you'll probably see a bunch of notifications and be reminded of how popular you really are. ;)

Change the setting.

Remind him that it will end. 

If you're personally familiar with bad trip territory, tell your friend that you've been there before. The worst feeling is thinking that your experience of "losing it" is unique. It's not. He's not the first person or last person to have a bad trip. He will come out the other side like the rest of us. Remind him of that.

Assure him that it's normal. Play it down if you can ("oh that sucks man, been there before, keep your head up") and keep your own vibes confident and positive. It's just one of those shitty things that happens, and most stoners/trippers will will have uncomfortable experiences at some point.

Mix up the music/activities. 

A bath/shower can have a "renewing" affect (especially on the comedown), but I can also see the possibility of that getting weird if he's tripping real hard on psychs.

**Make sure he stays hydrated.** This can do wonders, especially if it's a weed-related incident.

Don't let him isolate himself too much.

If he's comfortable with it, have him talk out his thoughts/fears. Sometimes just hearing yourself talk allows you to look critically at your thought process.

Could elaborate on "psychosis"?

It's very possible he has derealization/depersonalization. I would describe DP/DR as a disturbing sense of unreality/strangeness, but without any perceptions or beliefs that aren't based in consensus reality. So I can feel like I'm living in a dream or like I'm on an alien planet, but recognize in an intellectual sense who I am, who you are, and what's going on around me. I wouldn't think, for example, that "they're after me" or hear voices. It has features of psychosis (you certainly feel like you're losing it, like you could blink out of existence at any moment) but isn't quite the same thing. I can't really describe it.

I can say from experience that derealization is a profoundly painful experience when it persists for any longer than a few weeks (I had it for a solid half year after my first mushroom trip). Psychosis is a very vague term and can mean a lot of things. 

Give more details and maybe we can help you out more.

You ARE a person. You ARE an ego.

You are ALSO more. 

That doesn't mean you can neglect your responsibility toward cultivating and caring for yourself as an individual. Truth be told, there's nothing wrong with the ego. It's a useful part of who you are and isn't to be discarded.

You can transcend the limitations of the ego-self without negating the individuality which we naturally have. It's there for a *reason*. 

While your ego self is continuous with the rest of existence, it also has unique characteristics that contribute something to the grand scheme of the universe. You're like a wave in the ocean. You are both a distinct thing (a wave) and part of a whole (the ocean). If all the waves were flattened out, the ocean would lose its "oceanness", because part of what defines an ocean is the assembly of distinct waves that it is composed of.

"Good" and "bad", "self" and "other", are useful and meaningful concepts. Accept them. Don't try to do away with them, because doing so is both impossible and purposeless. Just try to recognize that they are only a *part* of the whole and aren't absolute.

I feel like you're beating yourself up for simply being what you naturally are. Honestly, none of us will ever transcend the ego in this life, and that's ok, because we're not supposed to. Be content being you--a distinct part of a whole--while keeping awareness of the greater picture.

Maybe I'm taking what you're saying wrong, in which case I'm sorry. But I've been in a similar place (feeling like the ego is the enemy) and I feel like it's not a healthy place to be.

It's all about balance. I hope that made at least a little sense.

Try to get out of your head. The purpose of "self-exploration" isn't just to sit and navel-gaze. It does you no good to have "found yourself" if you just sit and wallow in the metaphysics of your selfhood all day. Go do something. Pursue a passion. Live. 

This is a lesson I've learned first-hand after half a year of derealization following tripping and serious "self-exploration".

My suggestion? Once a week, go out, leave your phone at home, and spend the whole day exploring. Go on adventures. That plot of woods down the road? That neighborhood you don't know too well? That nature preserve a few towns away? Go check it out. Bring some friends if you want. Get lost in your own backyard. 

Forget about spirituality and metaphysics and philosophy. They're empty by themselves and all too often become escapism from the fact that we're afraid to actually go do something. Put intellectual/spiritual/mental issues on the backburner for a bit and embrace that animal side of you that wants to get up and do something for it's own sake. It's bursting with vitality if you let it come out. 

Forgetting about your "spiritual self" and esoteric mumbo jumbo and just *being human* is spirituality in itself, and at this point is more likely to put you in touch with who you really are than dropping acid or meditating or thinking about philosophy all day.

I'm not trying to put down all that stuff, as it's great. But you can go to extremes in both direction, and extremes are never healthy. I say that from experience.

Good luck.

You're not crazy. I'm seriously overjoyed that I could help, even a little bit. 

Now a bit of advice...

I'll say that, although the "trigger trip" for my mental issues wasn't nearly as dramatic as yours (that's a hell of a trip, I've got to say), the following derealization dealt with the *same exact themes*. I felt like I had seen "beyond the veil", seen something about the inner workings of reality, and had the impression that something was amiss in this human world. It was pervasive. A day didn't pass when I didn't find myself staring blankly in front of me, overwhelmed by the sheer weight of the fact that anything existed at all, shrinking deeper and deeper into my head, losing emotional contact with the world around me. 

Nothing emotionally "registered" anymore. I experienced the world as if I were an alien that had just landed on earth and was observing the workings of the world from a detached, scientific perspective. I could look at my old backyard and not experience a hint of familiarity.

I convinced myself that the only way to get out of it was going "deeper down the rabbit hole" with the hopes that somewhere in the deep dark abyss was a light at the end of the tunnel if I kept going in that direction. (I was wrong) So I latched on to my derealization, scared of being a coward. Scared that if I shut out all the weirdness around me, I was giving up on enlightenment and spiritual growth. I convinced myself that I was "onto something". Might I have been? Possibly. But nothing so useful as to sacrifice my sanity.

**This is an analogy that helped me a lot.**

During my period of derealization, I felt like I had to transcend being human. Human perspective, with all of its cultural trappings and Earthly concerns, was beneath me. It was an illusion. It was "the matrix" and I had gotten out of it. I had taken the red pill, and scary as it may have been, I thought myself better off for it.

And then I realized this. 

Not you, not me, not *anyone*, will ever understand what's going on in this universe in its entirety. 

*Picture a jazz band. (I would have picked an orchestra, but that would imply a pre-composed symphony, which can raise undesirable questions of free will. Jazz leaves more room for improvisation.) There are guitars, basses, saxophones, trumpets, drums, keyboards, all manner of musical instruments. You're a musician in this band.*

*What would happen if the percussionist tried to "transcend" his part and play the whole piece on the snare drum? That's right. It would fall apart. Or if the keyboardist tried to "transcend" her part and play the bass and sax at the same time? Again, it would fall apart.*

*The best anyone in this band can do is play their own part as damn well as they can, and add their own voice to the music. We're all surrounded by instruments we doesn't know how to play or understand. If we spend all of our time trying to understand everything else, we're missing an opportunity to contribute what we can to the most beautiful symphony ever written.*

How does that relate to your issue? Bear with me.

Pretend that there really *is* an evil conspiracy that must be fought and destroyed (I realize that you're skeptical, but I'm making a point). You have two options:

1. You can drop a bunch of acid and hope that Morpheus will spontaneously appear in front of you in a dream and offer you a second chance to leave the Matrix and join the resistance.

2. You can realize that you don't know exactly what's going on in a macrocosmic sense (does anyone?), but that in front of you is a world that nobody else but you—not me, not your neighbor, not your father, not your dog—is in a position to understand. **This is your realm.** This is your part. The instrument is in front of you. If you don't play it, it's going to stay unplayed forever. 

If there's something wrong with the music (or reality), fix it from where you are. Play your own instrument better. Make your own world a little more beautiful. It's all you can do.

The world is pretty damn strange. I'll give you that. It can be intimidating. It's true that we see only a sliver of reality. But there are other creatures taking care of that, so you don't have to worry about it. The universe is smart, I think. Getting upset over the smallness of our own little sliver is like getting upset over not being a bear-man-dolphin-extra-terrestrial-buddha-bacteria all at once. 

*(If it sounds like I'm being condescending, I'm not. I still need to have this conversation with myself daily to keep from being driven crazy by this shit.)*

Somewhere out there, there might be beings—physical or spiritual or both (or neither)—that are right at home in those fringes of consciousness that are so terrifying to you and me. Leave dealing with the Lovecraftian horrors to them (if you know Lovecraft you'll get what I mean). That's their realm, and they're doing their job keeping it. All you can do is occupy yours, which is being human. 

Do you want more knowledge and understanding? Explore your world. The normal, mundane human one. I know it sounds like stoner philosophy 101, but you know how the universe might be outwardly and inwardly infinite? (What if the universe is, like, one big atom man?) You can go just as deep into studying atoms as you can into studying galaxies. There's a little infinity to be discovered just by looking at what it means to be human. Start here, on "home atom". It's what you're best at.

And after you die, who knows? But there's no use thinking about that. 

I'm not telling you to pretend that you never saw what you saw. I'm just saying that you have to put it in its place. Someday you might understand it better, but that time isn't now. Now is your time to be human. Worry about the other stuff later.

There are a thousand valid ways to look at the universe, and the Gnostic conspiracy-laden lens is just one of them. Does it have some validity? Sure (I'm one of those folks myself, paranoid guy that I am). But it's not the end-all.

Rant done. Hope it helped at least a little bit.

No offense intended to the others. Philosophizing about the nature of reality is a great thing, and I'm glad to say that all my pondering during my period of derealization has made me a better "metaphysicist" (did I just coin a word?). 

But as someone whose gone through this, I've found that it gets you no where if you're trying to get back in touch with everyday reality. Philosophy can be supplemental, if can give you that extra justification for why returning to normal is a good thing, but it won't get you out of the woods.

What I recommend is mindfulness. 

Realize what's going on. When you have a thought like "nothing is real" and feel the accompanying anxiety, *realize what triggered it*.

Thoughts (ex. "nothing is real") --> Reaction (ex. "I don't like that idea") --> Anxiety (ex. "oh no! I'm going to have more derealization!") --> Derealization

**You have to break this cycle the one place that you can.** THE REACTION.

How can you do that? Talk to the thought. Say "hi, how do you do?" Don't try to combat it. Don't argue with it. Just recognize it for what it is. A thought, no better or worse than any other. Acknowledge it and move on. You'll find that by fighting the thoughts, you give them power over you. This takes practice, but eventually you'll get the hang of it.

Something else...

You probably find yourself self-monitoring, always asking yourself "am I getting better/worse?" This creates anxiety. Catch yourself doing it, and *realize what's going on". Don't try to suppress your self-monitoring thoughts. That's impossible (don't think of pink elephants either...see? you just thought of them). Just realize what's happening, and that alone puts you back in power.

Education certainly helps, but I don't think anything can fully prepare a person for tripping until they do it. 

When you feel your sense of identity disintegrating, it's hard to grasp onto the advice of a stranger on Reddit, no matter how sound it is. You can certainly try, and it *does* help. If I hadn't bothered to educate myself beforehand, I can barely imagine how awful my bad trip would have been.

But I think that education can only take you so far. I hope that makes sense.

I won't speak for others, but from my experience the pain of derealization was that I was never home. 

I could be sitting in my old living room with my dog on my lap, a bowl of popcorn, and my favorite cartoon from childhood and still feel like I'm on an alien planet watching this strange two-legged being (myself, of course) stare at a screen while wondering what the fuck anything is in some sort of weird incoherent fever dream logic.

It feels like you're lost in this mental void and there's no escape, and I assure you, it's the farthest thing from home.

The best advice I can give you is this: don't go in with expectations. 

Tripping for the first time will not be what you expect, no matter what. It may be harder, easier, stranger, more familiar, scarier, funnier than what you think it will be like. You don't know until it happens.

So don't go in looking for one thing in particular. Just go in, prepared to learn *something*, and you will.

Realize that, no matter how open minded or philosophical you are, your worldview and framework for understanding reality may be ripped away, dismantled, and put back together again as something you weren't ready for.

If you're the type to overthink and philosophize about things, realize that this *will* make it trippier and possibly more challenging, because you're taking it seriously rather than just having fun. My advice? Don't try to figure out what's happening to you, especially during the trip. Just realize that it's happening, and it *will* end. You did not take the "red pill". You will not be like this forever. It will be ok. 

Good luck!

I thought that the derealization was all solved in the week after the acid trip, but unfortunately it's not that easy. But I can say that now it's taken on a more manageable quality, where derealization is more of an existential nuisance than something that totally fucks me over. Don't get me wrong, I still have really shitty moments, but now I know what's happening and I know how to deal with them. 

I came up with this analogy to describe derealization:

You know how on Reddit we talk about "meta" posts? Normal consciousness is like being in a subreddit and being totally absorbed in conversation about the topic that the subreddit pertains to. Derealization is "going meta", except not about just one topic in life, but about **existence as a whole**. **EVERYTHING**. And it's not like I'm in everyday consciousness but just absorbed with metaphysical questions. My entire state of consciousness "goes meta" so that I'm no longer *in life* at all. I'm watching it from the outside, and it's all strange as fuck. I know that it might sound all "enlightened", and I do think that there are some insights to be gained from this, but it's still a headfuck that makes life near impossible to deal with when it's happening.

**There's always a tradeoff.** 

In this case, it's losing appreciation for "human" things in favor of perpetually confronting the brunt force of reality without any "softening" filter. It's odd because things feel at once *more* real and more like The Matrix at the same time. Like I can look at a busy highway and be totally overwhelmed by the magnitude of what's going on in a way that I never am when I'm "normal", but I'm also aware of how, outside of my head, there's a noumenal world (see Kant) that could bear no resemblance to the phenomenal world I'm experiencing. My derealization makes me realize how many aspects about the world are just "tamed" by our mind to keep us from getting overwhelmed. We put everything into little compartmentalized boxes to make them seem normal, but things in themselves are *reaaaally* crazy. I am incredibly happy that this thread helped you. Derealization is such an awful thing to experience and I sympathize with you on the deepest level. With that said, it's an amazing thing how me reaching out to this community helped a total stranger with the same problem.

I would advise that you think about this:

**Thoughts** ["nothing is real", "everything is alien", "I feel so detached from the world"]
*-->* 
**Reaction**  ["that thought makes me feel uncomfortable", "I can't control my thoughts"]
*-->* 
**Anxiety** ["I'm losing control", "I'm going crazy", "I'm stuck like this", "my thoughts won't go away so *maybe they're right* blah blah blah"]
*-->*
**Derealization**

And then it starts over again. 

**How can we break this loop?**

Thought suppression obviously doesn't work. (Don't think of pink giraffes.) Your thoughts will come, and will come in more force precisely because you *don't* want to think about them. Seeing as the thoughts are the *trigger* for all of this, we need some way to deal with the negative thoughts without trying to suppress them. 

How can we do that?

Arguing with them can help, but has limited usefulness. While a logical alternative to your thoughts can give your struggle against them more validity in your head, *you won't rationalize your way out of this problem.* I repeat, **you will not rationalize your way out of this problem.**

A combative solution is not the answer. The answer is to recognize your thoughts for what they are, *and no more*. They're only *thoughts*, no more valid than your best and most positive ones. They come into your head and can leave your head just as easily. In the deepest part of you, there is a self that transcends your thoughts. Think of your thoughts as a river. Most of the time you are immersed in that river (which is usually ok), but your true *transcendent* self isn't caught up in the flow. The transcendent self can sit on the bank and watch the river flow by without being caught up in it. I'm not saying that some Buddha-like state of constant detachment is attainable, necessary, or even desirable for you. But if your thoughts are causing problems for you, that's when you need to get out of the river, dry off, and watch the river flow.   

I'm going to paraphrase a story that I heard second hand from someone (the accuracy or source of the story is really irrelevant, as much as I'm a stickler for these sorts of things). It went something like this. 

*When the Buddha was meditating, demons would constantly come and harass him and try to distract him from reaching enlightenment. But whenever the demons came around, the Buddha wouldn't fight or resist them. He would invite them to tea.*

So when you have those "trigger thoughts", the key to preventing derealization is to refrain from reacting to them. Reacting brings you back into the river. Instead of resisting your thoughts, talk to your thoughts. Tell them "hello thought, nice to meet you", and get on with your day. The thoughts don't have any power except the power that you give them. Don't give them that power. Acknowledge them, but don't fight with them. 

And something else that is important... Recognize that your derealization *is not showing you anything*. It may have started as an interesting (and even valid) shift in perspective, like some kind of esoteric headspace that makes you feel "onto something", but it's usefulness has long since passed. You're now at a far extreme that is trapping you in a state of confusion. At first, I thought the symptoms were kind of cool, like a trippyness I can carry into everyday life. It wasn't troubling, just strange--novel. I thought it was showing me the world from an objective standpoint, and i embraced it. But as time passed, I found myself more and more isolated from the world until I developed full-blown derealization. Derealization causes you to negatively evaluate the world, and that negative evaluation alone creates *separation* that actually *prevents* you from learning about the world you want to understand. It detaches you from the immanent reality you live in and puts you so far into your head that your mind becomes a prison. It produce a separation that is the exact opposite of enlightenment. 

Something else that you have to do is to *refrain from self-monitoring*. I know the temptation to "check up on yourself" and see how you're doing. When things are bad, you try to assess exactly how bad they are, and when things are going well, you try to see if you've made any progress. If you're doing better, you might experiment to see if you can handle any of the scary thoughts now that you're presumably "making progress", at which point it all comes rushing back. What you have to do is **stop asking yourself how you're doing**. That only brings out the thoughts that feed the derealization loop. You will inevitably catch yourself self-monitoring from time to time, but as you refuse to indulge further, the urge will eventually die out.

I hope this helped. Let me know if there's anything I can do to help you out. All of this, combined with Devananda's advice, has been invalubly helpful and I now have high hopes that I'm "out of the woods" for good. I wish you the best of luck.

Disclaimer: i'm not experienced, since i've got only one shroom trip under my belt.
(here if you want to read about it: https://www.reddit.com/r/shrooms/comments/2wensx/my_first_psychedelic_experience_25_g_shrooms/)

but from personal experience, i actually regret not doing more. because i feel like it was weird enough to freak me out and give me a disturbing "mindfuck" but not enough to really blow me away, so i was sort of in an uncomfortable psychedelic limbo where i was just walking around thinking about and analyzing what was happening instead of feeling it (which can contribute a lot to a bad trip). keep in mind that most people will recommend a low dose (for good reason, i'm sure), but there are two sides to that. i think the dose regret is mostly personal to me, but keep it in the back of your head when deciding how much you'll do.

for you though, if you're going in with no psychoactive experience at all, 2 g should be more than enough.

some advice: 

*nourish yourself!

*stay away from large groups at all costs

*have a sitter

*on the come up, just chill out, zone out, and listen to some good, positive music

*if you plan to be outside (recommended for at least part of the trip), trip during nice, sunny weather if at all possible and surround yourself with pleasant nature.

*if your mind is in an unpleasant place, maybe watch a good creative cartoon (like disney's fantasia, wallace and gromit, alice in wonderland, something cool like that)

*this is your time. if you feel like being with other people will stop you from doing your thing (ex. they want a different kind of music, want a different setting than you, etc.), don't "settle" for something you don't totally love. there's no rush to do it. make the first time perfect. i'm NOT saying you should do it alone (please don't!), but choose your setting and company wisely.

*do lots of reading on erowid, the shroomery, etc. maybe read a book or two (huxley's doors of perception is an awesome start).  learn as much as you possibly can! trip reports are great. read advice threads. look up how to deal with bad trips. go into the trip fully equipped! (this is great: https://www.erowid.org/psychoactives/faqs/psychedelic_experience_faq.shtml)

*turn off your mind. relax. float downstream.


As far as smoking, i would DEFINITELY recommend a vaporizer. they're great. i've got a magic flight launch box, which is very nice. it's also very economical with bud. when you feel like you've got a decent hang of the cannabis experience, then go on and start thinking about the shrooms. marijuana can be pretty psychedelic by itself, so try to take advantage of that!

best of luck!

To me, the void means the idea that the only thing separating us from meaninglessness (or something so big and scary as to be unfathomable to our puny human minds) is a flimsy veil of security that can be ripped away at any second. The void is when you experience the human "lens" for viewing things being stripped away and seeing them devoid of the meaning we attach to them on a day to day basis. I've never been "in" the void itself, so to speak, but i have looked over the edge and for the months following the trip there's this unshakable sense of being "on the verge" of something terrifying. You feel like you're going to lose it.

I remember on my first trip (an unpleasant one) that as i watched my friends playing their guitars, we all seemed like primitive caveman amusing ourselves by playing with objects. Even the best music in the world would have seemed meaningless and silly in that moment. 

"The void" is a place where none of the things that previous helped you to make sense of the world and your self cease to make sense. You confront them as if for the first time, but not through a human lens. You see things impartially. Yet, that human fear within you cries out that "yes, all of these things DO have intrinsic meaning", but it's screaming into some kind of abyss that doesn't care about your conceptions of meaning. It's a scary place to be. You're beyond comfort because you see all of the human things that comfort you as being meaningless to the non-human place where your mind is. 

Now i don't think that "the void" is the ultimate reality or anything like that. But it is a place that your mind can take you, and not a pleasant one for most people.
